title: AI Benchmarking: A Working Reference
description: What an AI benchmark can and cannot tell you, and the practices that make a score trustworthy.

scope.objective: Explain what an AI benchmark can and cannot tell you, and set out the practices that make a score trustworthy.
excludes: hardware and systems benchmarking beyond the MLPerf governance comparison
scope.evidenceBoundary: Public papers, benchmark documentation, standards text, and vendor methodology pages read on 2026-08-11.

evidenceStates.meaning: Stated by a named source; not independently checked
evidenceStates.howItAppears: The default for benchmark item counts and vendor methodology

evidenceStates.meaning: Recomputed here from a disclosed formula and stated inputs
Expected but not confirmed against a source read for this report
evidenceStates.howItAppears: Written as n/v, never as zero or a guess

evidenceStates.meaning: Reasoned from the sources rather than stated by any one of them
evidenceStates.howItAppears: Flagged in the text with wording such as "the mechanism generalises"

statisticalChecks.description: Standard error of 71.2% accuracy over 500 independent items
Upper bound of the 95% interval for the same score
Questions needed to detect a 3-point difference at 80% power, 5% significance, omega squared 1/9
Minimum detectable effect for 500 items with per-item difference sd 0.5
Unbiased pass@5 from 10 samples with 3 correct
Unbiased pass@1 from 10 samples with 3 correct
50% raw on a 4-option benchmark, normalised so chance maps to 0

rules.rule: Name the construct before the task
rules.why: A benchmark that claims to measure "reasoning" but scores multiple-choice recall will be read as the former and used as the former
Prompt, temperature, sampling count, answer extraction, and scoring code each change the number

rules.rule: Put an error bar on every score
rules.why: Without one, a reader cannot tell a real gain from run-to-run variation

rules.rule: Compare models per question, not per average
rules.why: Paired differences are free precision, roughly a third less variance at a typical correlation

rules.rule: Assume the public test set leaked
rules.why: Then design around it: private splits, fresh items, and dated problems

rules.rule: Retire a benchmark when it saturates
rules.why: A score of 96% with a 6% label-error rate measures the labels, not the model

rules.rule: Calibrate every automated judge against humans
rules.why: A model grader has known, measurable biases; agreement with experts is the only defence

rules.rule: Report cost and reliability beside accuracy
rules.why: An agent that wins by calling the model 50 times is not better, it is more expensive

rules.rule: Verify the grader before trusting the task
rules.why: Most agent-benchmark inflation comes from the checker, not the tasks

rules.rule: Write down what the benchmark cannot tell you
rules.why: The limitation section is the part a decision-maker needs and the part usually missing

benchmarks.name: MMLU
benchmarks.notes: An audit found errors in 6.49% of questions, and 57% of the analysed virology questions (Gema et al. 2024)

benchmarks.name: MMLU-Redux
benchmarks.notes: The corrected subset of MMLU, across all 57 subjects

benchmarks.name: MMLU-Pro
benchmarks.notes: Ten options lower the chance baseline from 25% to 10%

benchmarks.name: ARC (AI2 Reasoning Challenge)
benchmarks.notes: Was in the first Open LLM Leaderboard suite

benchmarks.name: HellaSwag
benchmarks.notes: Was in the first Open LLM Leaderboard suite

benchmarks.name: Winogrande
benchmarks.notes: Was in the first Open LLM Leaderboard suite

benchmarks.name: TruthfulQA
benchmarks.notes: Measures imitation of common falsehoods, not general truthfulness

benchmarks.name: BIG-bench
benchmarks.notes: Introduced the canary string convention for contamination control

benchmarks.name: BIG-Bench Hard (BBH)
benchmarks.notes: The subset where models scored below the human rater average

benchmarks.name: GPQA
benchmarks.notes: Expert-written; validated so that non-experts with web access and 30 minutes cannot solve them

benchmarks.name: MuSR
benchmarks.notes: Added in the second Open LLM Leaderboard suite

benchmarks.name: IFEval
benchmarks.notes: Constraints such as "reply in exactly three bullet points" are verified by code, not a judge

benchmarks.name: Humanity's Last Exam (HLE)
benchmarks.notes: Questions were adversarially filtered against several frontier models, so those models should not be compared directly against later ones

benchmarks.name: ARC-AGI-2
benchmarks.notes: Keeps a private evaluation set; targets composition and rule application rather than knowledge

benchmarks.name: GSM8K
benchmarks.grader: Exact match on the final number
benchmarks.notes: The canonical example of a benchmark that stopped discriminating

benchmarks.name: MATH
benchmarks.notes: The Level 5 subset and the MATH-500 subset are both still quoted

benchmarks.name: Mock AIME 2024-2025
benchmarks.notes: Built by Epoch AI as a harder replacement once MATH Level 5 saturated

benchmarks.name: FrontierMath
benchmarks.items: 338 (295 in Tiers 1 to 3, 43 in Tier 4), 12 published as samples
benchmarks.format: Research-level problems with a single checkable answer
benchmarks.notes: Version 2, released 12 June 2026, corrected 123 Tier 1 to 3 problems and 12 Tier 4 problems and removed 12 after an audit found errors affecting 42% of the original set. OpenAI funded the benchmark and holds access to a subset, disclosed on the benchmark page

benchmarks.name: HumanEval
benchmarks.format: Write a Python function from a docstring
benchmarks.notes: Introduced the pass@k estimator used across the field

benchmarks.name: MBPP
benchmarks.notes: Often quoted alongside HumanEval

benchmarks.name: SWE-bench
benchmarks.notes: Drawn from public repositories that model providers train on

benchmarks.name: SWE-bench Verified
benchmarks.notes: Human-validated by OpenAI to remove wrong grading, underspecified issues, and over-specific tests. OpenAI has since said it no longer measures frontier coding capability

benchmarks.name: LiveCodeBench
benchmarks.items: Grows continuously; a 2025 release covered 1,055 problems (n/v)
benchmarks.format: Contest programming problems tagged with a publication date
benchmarks.notes: Scores only problems published after a model's training cutoff, which is contamination control by timestamp

benchmarks.name: Terminal-Bench
benchmarks.format: Complete a job in a Linux shell
benchmarks.notes: Carries a large weight in the Artificial Analysis coding category

benchmarks.name: KernelBench
benchmarks.notes: One of the ten benchmarks audited for validity failures by the Agentic Benchmark Checklist

benchmarks.name: SciCode
benchmarks.notes: Used in the Artificial Analysis coding category

benchmarks.name: GAIA
benchmarks.format: Assistant questions needing browsing, files, and tools, in three difficulty levels
benchmarks.notes: Answers for the test split are withheld and scored by submission

benchmarks.name: WebArena
benchmarks.format: Multi-step tasks on self-hosted clones of real websites
benchmarks.notes: Audited for validity failures by the Agentic Benchmark Checklist

benchmarks.name: OSWorld
benchmarks.format: Control a real desktop by mouse and keyboard
benchmarks.notes: Audited for validity failures by the Agentic Benchmark Checklist

benchmarks.name: τ-bench
benchmarks.format: Customer-service conversation with tools and a policy document
benchmarks.notes: Introduced pass^k, the share of tasks solved in every one of k attempts. Reported that a leading model of the time solved under 50% of tasks and under 25% consistently across 8 attempts

benchmarks.name: τ²-bench
benchmarks.format: Same idea across airline, retail, and telecom, with the user also acting
benchmarks.notes: Adds a second actor, so the agent must coordinate rather than just execute

benchmarks.name: MLE-bench
benchmarks.format: Build a machine-learning solution end to end
benchmarks.notes: Grading is inherited from Kaggle, which removes grader design risk

benchmarks.name: Cybench
benchmarks.format: Solve security challenges in a sandbox
benchmarks.notes: Used as a safety-relevant capability eval, including on the Holistic Agent Leaderboard

benchmarks.name: CVE-Bench
benchmarks.format: Exploit real web vulnerabilities in a sandbox
benchmarks.notes: The Agentic Benchmark Checklist cut its performance overestimate by 33%

benchmarks.name: CORE-bench
benchmarks.format: Reproduce the computational results of a published paper
benchmarks.notes: Measures reproducibility work rather than invention

benchmarks.name: GDPval
benchmarks.format: Produce a real work deliverable, such as a legal brief or a nursing care plan
benchmarks.grader: Blinded pairwise expert comparison against a human deliverable
benchmarks.notes: Task authors averaged about 14 years of professional experience. The grader is a human expert who does not know which deliverable is the model's

benchmarks.name: AgentHarm
benchmarks.notes: A refusal-and-capability eval rather than a capability-only one

suites.name: HELM
suites.composition: 42 scenarios, with 7 metrics measured on 16 core scenarios
suites.notes: Raised the share of core scenarios that a typical model had been measured on from 17.9% to 96.0%, and publishes every prompt and completion

suites.name: Open LLM Leaderboard
suites.composition: First suite: ARC, HellaSwag, MMLU, TruthfulQA, Winogrande, GSM8K. Second suite from June 2024: MMLU-Pro, GPQA, MuSR, IFEval, BBH, MATH Level 5
suites.notes: The second suite normalises each score so that chance performance maps to 0 and perfect to 100 before averaging. The whole leaderboard was later archived

suites.name: Chatbot Arena (LMArena)
suites.whatItIs: Crowd preference voting between anonymous model pairs
suites.grader: Human votes, fitted with a Bradley-Terry model
suites.notes: Ratings come with bootstrap confidence intervals, and the top few models usually overlap

suites.name: MT-Bench
suites.notes: The judge agreed with human raters more than 80% of the time, about the same as humans agreed with each other

suites.name: Arena-Hard
suites.whatItIs: Harder automatic prompts distilled from arena traffic
suites.notes: Built to correlate with arena rankings at much lower cost

suites.name: AlpacaEval, length-controlled
suites.grader: Model judge with a length correction
suites.notes: Exists because judges prefer longer answers, so the raw version rewarded verbosity

suites.name: Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index
suites.composition: Version 4.1.1 combines 9 evaluations in 4 categories: Agents 34%, Coding 24%, Scientific Reasoning 24%, General 18%
suites.notes: Publishes repeat counts per evaluation (1 to 5), temperature settings, and cost and latency per task beside the score

suites.name: Holistic Agent Leaderboard (HAL)
suites.whatItIs: A third-party, cost-aware agent leaderboard with one shared harness
suites.notes: Validated with 21,730 agent attempts across 9 models and 9 benchmarks for about $40,000, with all logs published

suites.name: Epoch AI Benchmarking Hub
suites.whatItIs: An independent re-runner of selected benchmarks
suites.composition: Runs GPQA Diamond, MATH Level 5, Mock AIME, FrontierMath, SWE-bench Verified itself
suites.notes: Runs 16 samples per question on GPQA Diamond and Mock AIME, 8 on MATH Level 5, and shows plus or minus one standard error

suites.name: MLPerf
suites.whatItIs: Systems benchmarking for training and inference
suites.notes: Governance worth copying: a Closed division that fixes the model and optimiser, an Open division that must document every deviation, and up to two audited submissions per round

failureModes.symptom: A percentage to one or two decimals, no interval, no n
failureModes.fix: Publish the standard error and n

failureModes.failure: Ranking on gaps smaller than the noise
failureModes.symptom: "Slightly ahead", "narrowly leads", table sorted by a 0.4-point gap
failureModes.fix: Report the paired difference and its interval; call overlapping results indistinguishable

failureModes.failure: Numbers from different harnesses in one table
failureModes.symptom: Footnotes citing several different papers for one column
failureModes.fix: Re-run every system yourself under one harness, or do not put them in one table

failureModes.symptom: The write-up has no section describing what the result cannot support
failureModes.fix: Write the limitation section; it is the part a decision-maker needs

failureModes.symptom: A benchmark whose top scorer also paid for it, with no conflict statement
failureModes.fix: Disclose funding, access, and data-use terms at publication

failureModes.symptom: The benchmark set was chosen by the party making the claim, and no unfavourable benchmark appears
failureModes.fix: Ask who chose the suite; require a pre-registered set or a standard one

failureModes.symptom: Only one variant's score is published, with no count of how many were tried
failureModes.fix: Disclose every run including withdrawn ones, or limit submissions per version

failureModes.symptom: The suite is also the development target, with no held-out split
failureModes.fix: Hold back a split you rarely look at; the gap is your overfitting estimate

failureModes.symptom: A reading-comprehension or multilingual benchmark reporting a plain standard error
failureModes.fix: Cluster on the sampled unit; the correction reached 3x on a real eval

failureModes.symptom: Two averages with separate intervals, no per-question analysis
failureModes.fix: Take per-question differences; roughly a third less variance for free

failureModes.symptom: A 200-item benchmark used to argue a 2-point improvement
failureModes.fix: Compute the minimum detectable effect first

failureModes.failure: Temperature lowered to steady the numbers
failureModes.symptom: "We used temperature 0 to reduce variance"
failureModes.fix: Do not. It can triple the irreducible spread and shift the mean

failureModes.failure: Standard error pooled over all samples
failureModes.symptom: An interval that shrinks when they resample the same questions more
failureModes.fix: Compute the error across question-level means

failureModes.failure: Averaging benchmarks with different chance baselines
failureModes.symptom: A mean of a 4-option multiple-choice score and a free-text score
failureModes.fix: Normalise chance to 0 and perfect to 100 before averaging

failureModes.symptom: A "Total" row under a column of rates
failureModes.fix: Total only additive, non-overlapping counts

failureModes.symptom: A single "intelligence" number with no published composition
failureModes.fix: Publish the components and their weights

failureModes.failure: Construct named broader than the task
failureModes.symptom: A multiple-choice set presented as measuring "reasoning"
failureModes.fix: State the construct and what it excludes; describe the task in the claim

failureModes.symptom: The answer is reachable from a file in the environment, or from the question's phrasing
failureModes.fix: Run the shortcut hunt; audits found up to 100% relative overstatement

failureModes.symptom: An empty or truncated output scored as success
failureModes.fix: Negative controls: empty, wrong, and partial outputs must all fail

failureModes.failure: Answer-extraction failures counted as model failures
failureModes.symptom: A correct answer in an unexpected format scored wrong
failureModes.fix: Publish and test the extraction rule; report extraction failures separately

failureModes.symptom: "Above human level" with no description of which humans, or how long they had
failureModes.fix: State who the humans were, their expertise, and their conditions

failureModes.failure: Public test set treated as evidence of generalisation
failureModes.symptom: A claim about generalisation on a benchmark that has been on the open web for two years
failureModes.fix: Use a private split, dated items, or a fresh set

failureModes.failure: Saturated benchmark still used to rank
failureModes.symptom: Top models within a point of each other, near the ceiling
failureModes.fix: Retire it, or report it as a floor check only

failureModes.failure: Model judge with no human calibration
failureModes.symptom: A model-graded score with no agreement rate reported
failureModes.fix: Hold out human labels, report agreement, re-check after any judge change

failureModes.failure: Judge shares lineage with a contestant, or order effects uncontrolled
failureModes.symptom: One provider's model both competes and grades; single-order comparisons
failureModes.fix: Use an independent judge family; swap positions and require the win to survive both

failureModes.symptom: An agent leaderboard with one accuracy column
failureModes.fix: Report cost per task and pass^k, and plot accuracy against cost

glossary.definition: The share of items scored correct. Only meaningful alongside the number of items and the chance baseline
A system that takes several steps on its own: reading, calling tools, changing state, and deciding when to stop
See scaffold
A benchmark whose items are multi-step jobs in an environment, graded on the outcome rather than a single answer
Turning per-item scores into one number. The step where different chance baselines and unlike groups get illegally averaged
The rule that pulls a gradeable answer out of free-form model text. A frequent source of correct answers scored wrong
A family of abstract visual puzzle benchmarks that keeps a private evaluation set
A fixed set of tasks plus a fixed way of scoring them, used to compare systems
The observation that which method looks best depends heavily on which benchmarks the field happens to use
A statistical model that estimates one strength number per competitor from pairwise win and loss records. Used to turn arena votes into ratings
A unique marker embedded in a benchmark so that anyone can search a training corpus for it, or ask a model to reproduce it, as a contamination check
A test of whether a system can do something. Contrast with propensity evaluation
The score a system gets by guessing. 25% on a 4-option multiple-choice benchmark, 10% on a 10-option one, 0% on free text
In MLPerf, a submission category that fixes the model, optimiser, and data handling so that only the system underneath varies. Contrast with Open division
An error bar corrected for items that arrive in groups, such as several questions about one passage. On real evals the correction has reached a factor of three
A range that would contain the true value a stated share of the time if the experiment were repeated. Usually quoted at 95%
The ability or property a benchmark claims to measure, such as "multi-step arithmetic reasoning"
Whether the test measures the construct it claims to measure. Borrowed from psychometrics
Test material reaching a model during training, so its score partly reflects memorisation
Which parts of the construct, population, or risk taxonomy the benchmark actually touches, and which it does not
Whether the score predicts the real-world outcome you care about
A test of whether a model can do something harmful, run to inform a deployment or safeguard decision
Structured documentation for a dataset: motivation, composition, collection method, and recommended uses
Removing or excluding test items from training data, or filtering results to items known to postdate training
The effort spent getting a model to show a capability: prompting, tools, scaffolds, step budgets, and permitted fine-tuning. Central to safety evaluation
A rating system for pairwise contests. Arena ratings are often called Elo but are usually fitted with a Bradley-Terry model
Reading a sample of real outputs, writing down what went wrong in each, then grouping and counting. The standard first step in building an in-house suite
One run of an evaluation against one system. Also used loosely for the evaluation itself
A model recognising that it is being tested, which weakens any test of how it behaves when it thinks nobody is watching
The infrastructure that runs an evaluation end to end: supplies prompts and tools, runs items, records transcripts, grades, and aggregates
A collection of tasks assembled to measure a specific set of capabilities or behaviours
Showing the model worked examples in the prompt before the real item. The number, choice, and order of examples all move scores
A threshold in continuous integration that blocks a release when an evaluation criterion regresses
When a measure becomes a target, it stops being a good measure. The one-line summary of benchmark gaming
The logic that scores an attempt. Code-based, model-based, or human
The reference answer or outcome a grader compares against. Wrong ground truth caps a benchmark's usefulness
Items withheld from public release, or from your own tuning, so that a score on them measures generalisation
Measuring several properties, such as accuracy, calibration, robustness, bias, and efficiency, on the same scenarios rather than accuracy alone
How well people do on the same items, under stated conditions. Required for any "human level" claim
How often two human raters give the same verdict. Low agreement means the task is underspecified, not that the systems are similar
One scored unit of a benchmark: a question, a problem, or a task
Using a language model to grade open-ended outputs. Cheap, scalable, and biased in catalogued ways
A benchmark item whose recorded correct answer is wrong. Sets the ceiling above which scores are meaningless
Wall-clock time to complete an item. Report the median and a tail percentile, not the mean alone
A ranked table of systems. Its composition, harness, and submission policy matter more than its order
Correcting a judge's preference for longer answers, either statistically or by capping length
A benchmark that adds fresh items over time to resist contamination. Needs version pinning to stay comparable
Scoring a multiple-choice item by the model's probability for each option token rather than by parsing generated text. Gives different numbers from generation, and the two are not comparable
The smallest difference an evaluation can reliably detect at a given size and power. Compute it before drawing conclusions
Short structured documentation for a trained model: intended use, evaluation conditions, and performance broken down by group and condition
Rescaling scores so that chance maps to 0 and perfect to 100, so that benchmarks with different chance baselines can be averaged
In MLPerf, a submission category that permits changes to the workload provided every deviation is documented
Whether the grader reports success exactly when the task was actually solved
Comparing two systems item by item and analysing the differences, rather than comparing two averages. Reduces variance for free
The probability that at least one of k attempts succeeds. Estimated without bias as 1 minus C(n-c, k) / C(n, k) from n samples with c correct
The share of tasks solved in every one of k attempts. The reliability metric for unattended deployment
A judge preferring whichever answer it sees first. Fixed by running both orders and requiring the win to survive both
The probability that an experiment detects a real difference of a given size. Conventionally set at 80%
Items the benchmark holder never publishes, so providers cannot train on them. The strongest contamination defence and the greatest concentration of trust
Score changes caused by formatting choices that do not change meaning. Measured at up to 76 accuracy points on one open model
A test of whether a system will do something when it has the choice. Contrast with capability evaluation
Every setting that produces a score: prompt template, system prompt, examples, temperature, samples per item, tools, and step limits
Open-ended adversarial probing by people trying to break the system. Produces findings, not a score
A known-good answer or outcome for an item. Proves the item is solvable and lets you test the grader
Answering each item K times and averaging the per-item scores, to reduce the model's own answer noise
Deliberately withdrawing a benchmark once it saturates, contaminates, or hits its label-error ceiling
The share of judging decisions that survive an irrelevant change to the input. Used to quantify judge bias
Explicit written criteria a grader applies. Best used one dimension at a time
A model performing worse than it can, which makes a capability evaluation understate risk
Frontier scores bunching near a benchmark's ceiling, so it no longer separates systems
The code around a model that turns it into an agent: prompts, tool wiring, retries, and step limits. Two systems with the same model and different scaffolds are not comparable
A model judge preferring text produced by its own model family
A way to pass a task without the ability being tested. The main threat to task validity
The expected spread of an estimate. For accuracy p on n independent items, the square root of p times (1 minus p) divided by n
Whether an observed difference is larger than would be expected from noise alone, at a stated threshold
The imaginary larger pool of questions a benchmark's items are treated as a sample from. The assumption that makes error bars meaningful
Whether a task is solvable if and only if the system has the target ability
A sampling setting that controls output randomness. Do not change it to tidy up error bars
Testing, evaluation, verification, and validation. The term NIST uses for the measurement work in its risk framework
The length of task, measured by how long a human expert takes, that a model completes with a stated success rate
The complete record of one attempt: outputs, tool calls, intermediate results, and reasoning. Also called a trace or trajectory
One attempt at one task. Multiple trials per task are needed because behaviour varies between runs
A judge preferring longer answers regardless of quality
Giving the model the task with no worked examples in the prompt

limitations: No benchmark was run for this report; every quantitative claim about a model or benchmark is source-reported.
Benchmark composition, leaderboard rules, and index weights change monthly; version-specific statements are a snapshot of 2026-08-11.
Coverage skews to language and agent models, and to English-language work.
The regulatory section summarises and links to primary text; it is not legal advice.
Seventeen quotable claims rest on a secondary reading, listed in secondaryClaims.
